entries.title: Morgan Park showcases its aerial attack in Payton win
entries.summary: <p>Morgan Park opened the season with challenging road trips to Downers Grove North and Edwardsville and a matchup with Notre Dame. The Mustangs emerged with two wins and a five-point, resume-building loss to ranked Downers North.</p><p>For coach Chris James, the challenge now is keeping his team’s level high in Public League play.</p><p>“I’m not as worried about it as I used to be,” James said. “We do a lot now, as much as we can, to prohibit anything slipping. We used to play bad against teams we should beat, but we are getting better at that.”</p><p>Morgan Park knocked off Payton 61-7 on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/10/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Saturday</a> at Stagg Stadium.</p><p>The Mustangs ran the ball well over the first three weeks of the season so the focus against Payton was on junior quarterback Ronald Smith Jr. throwing the ball.</p><p>It was a success. Smith was 10-for-13 passing for 221 yards with three touchdowns and one interception.</p><p>He connected with Jeremiah Harvey for a 42-yard TD, Travezz Jones for a 33-yard TD, and Mark Dossous Jr. on an 11-yard score. Jones had four catches for 94 yards.</p><p>“I’m feeling good,” Smith said. “We have been progressing every week. We made a few mistakes the first week and then got better. We still have to improve, though.”</p><p>Senior running back William Smith Jr. opened the scoring with a 72-yard TD run, and Kenneth Sims ripped off a 57-yard TD run in the third quarter.</p><p>Linebacker Raymond Gilbert junior led the defensive effort for Morgan Park (3-1, 1-0 Red Star) with a couple of sacks and a fumble recovery.</p><p>Payton turned the ball over seven times. entries.title: Chief Keef Live 2026 Tour concert in Chicago postponed
entries.summary: <p>Saturday was supposed to be a landmark day for Chief Keef fans. </p><p>Fans from Chicago and beyond arrived at Huntington Bank Pavilion at Northerly Island in their best outfits to see the rapper's first show within the city limits in more than a decade.</p><p>As massive groups of spectators lined up in front of the entrance for the Chief Keef Live 2026 Tour kickoff concert, the venue posted a message on its <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DdNISDVj9JS/" target="_blank" >Instagram account</a> around 6 p.m. that the show was delayed. About an hour later, another message appeared saying Keef would not be performing at all. </p><p>"Chief Keef’s September 12th performance at Huntington Bank Pavilion has been postponed," the post read. "All previously purchased tickets will be honored for the new date."</p><p>Neither the venue nor Keef representatives provided a reason for the cancellation. </p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back with Sun-Times.com for updates. </i> </p>

entries.title: Will Venable ready to adjust as needed as White Sox try to shake late-season funk
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS, Mo. – With losses in nine of their last 12 games and their division lead shaved down to the bone, the announcement of Saturday’s White Sox lineup seemed to reveal the kind of major shake-up for which the offense’s September struggles had been calling.</p><p>Colson Montgomery and Braden Montgomery–both entering Saturday with an OPS under .600 for the month–were shifted to the bottom two spots of the order. Kyle Teel, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/10/slowed-by-injury-white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel-still-has-tools-for-a-breakout-will-venable-ryan-fuller-bat-speed-chris-getz" target="_blank" ><u>projected preseason to be a middle of the order fixture</u></a> but easing back from an ankle injury, was moved up to second.</p><p>Instead, manager Will Venable defused such notions of a big, reactive change.</p><p>"The change in lineup is not about performance or anything,” Venable said.</p><p>Near the end of Year 2 of the White Sox under Venable’s stewardship, it’s imprudent to assume he’s trying to send a message through the lineup when platoon matchups are the more likely explanation. Sure enough, his expectation that the Cardinals were planning to piggyback right-handed starter Kyle Leahy with left-hander Cooper Hjerpe drove a strategy geared around left-handed bats at the top of the order.</p><p>Of course, with the White Sox fighting for their playoff lives, there’s a world where this order has some staying power.</p><p>“Maybe we score a bunch of runs and we want to keep it exactly the same,” Venable quipped.</p><p>But is there a major adjustment coming as the White Sox suffer through their worst baseball of the season at a decidedly inopportune time? The window for a proactive response to the second half fades of Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami, even spitfire rookie leadoff man Sam Antonacci, has closed. Caleb Bonemer and his 37 minor league home runs could be an intriguing option next year, but there’s no late-season offensive impact waiting for the call in Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>“We played together all year, the vibes aren’t down,” said Chase Meidroth. “We have to move forward and find a way to win.”</p><p>Hitting coach Derek Shomon is grinding through adjustments in the batting cage, but from a deployment perspective, there’s not many transformative options. Instead Venable has largely kept the faith with his existing core, and his players echo the same steady confidence. What this Sox roster lacks in postseason experience, they make up for in experience in absorbing losses and trusting things will get better.</p><p>“There's been parts of the season where we weren't pitching well, we weren't hitting well, we weren't doing this or we weren't doing that,” Davis Martin told the Sun-Times. “We came out of it every time.”</p><p>“We know things are going to pass and we are going to get back on track when we need to,” said Colson Montgomery.</p><p>The question obviously also extends to the pitching staff, especially where using Sean Newcomb as an opener in front of him did little to stanch <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/11/white-sox-starter-luis-castillo-feels-hes-very-very-close-to-righting-ship-after-working-on-mechanics-colson-montgomery-strikeout-record-chase-meidroth-joey-bart-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>the bleeding from trade deadline acquisition Luis Castillo</u></a>. Newcomb, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/white-sox-sean-newcomb-starter-or-reliever-bullpen-will-venable-grant-taylor-sean-burke-free-agency-chris-getz-rotation-relief" target="_blank" ><u>the heavily-used rock of the bullpen all year long</u></a>, has now been charged with runs in four-straight outings, even though Saturday night was a case of Castillo allowing an inherited run to score, as the right-hander saw his velocity drop into the low-90s, was pulled after less than three innings of work and now has a 7.76 ERA in a White Sox uniform</p><p>The Sox do have starting pitching options in the minors that could be worth exploring, and that could begin as soon as Sunday. Venable contends that if anything, he’s ready to respond to how his players are performing in the moment more than ever.</p><p>“If we’re in early-April, May baseball, you’re kind of spreading out the love, spreading out the opportunity to make sure guys are plugged in,” Venable said. “Now it’s just about one day, and today, and how you’re going to win that game.”</p><p>During this skid, Venable has spent some postgame sessions lamenting moves that haven’t worked out, but insists he’s not hesitant to pull the trigger on some new ones going forward.</p><p>“If there's adjustments that are necessary,” Venable said, “We're going to make them.”<br></p>

entries.title: Westinghouse cruises past Curie
entries.summary: <p>Westinghouse missed the IHSA playoffs last year and were dropped from the Public League's top Red division to the second tier this season.</p><p>Neither development sat well with the Warriors, who are aiming to reestablish themselves as an upper-level team in the city.</p><p>"It definitely put a little chip on our shoulder for sure," junior two-way standout Ethan Wiley said.</p><p>Saturday's 42-6 romp past Curie at Rockne Stadium was a step in the right direction.</p><p>Senior Jaidyn Gandy ran nine times for 132 yards — all in the first half — including touchdowns of one and 50 yards. Wiley had five carries for 35 yards and a score. Bernard Mitchell Jr. also had a 50-yard touchdown run.</p><p>Gandy, who also runs track, moved from receiver to running back this season.</p><p>"He's been getting better every week, just working, learning different things," Westinghouse coach Julius Carter said.</p><p>"I love it," Gandy said of the switch. "Just anything to help the team. I know Coach is going to put me in the best possible position to succeed, and I just trust in that."</p><p>He does have previous experience at running back, so the position is not completely foreign to him.</p><p>"We've just got to be a football player at the end of the day," Gandy said.</p><p>Meanwhile, Carter said, "Ethan Wiley is probably one of the best players in the Public League. He's underrated, most definitely."</p><p>Wiley made the All-City team as a sophomore last year.</p><p>"He's a receiver, DB, whatever we need him at," Carter said. "He can do it all — run the ball, he's all-around, just an athlete."</p><p>"I definitely feel like I've got a lot to prove because there's a lot of guys out here [who are] getting way more exposed," Wiley said. "And I know I'm better than them. So yeah, I feel like it's a lot to prove out here."</p><p>Though they're still a win shy of their 2025 total, the Warriors (3-1, 1-0) are IHSA playoff-eligible this season under the expanded postseason format. But they still have a lot to play for in the regular season, even as they are missing some key players who are hurt.</p><p>"We still want to finish strong," Carter said. "The goal was to win conference, make the city and state playoffs and just keep things going in the right direction. So even with the injuries, that's the goal."</p><p>Curie (2-2, 0-1), which was shut out by Lincoln Park last week, also is navigating some injury issues. On Saturday, turnovers were a problem and led to three of Westinghouse's seven touchdowns.</p><p>One bright spot for the Condors was freshman backup quarterback Treyveon Townsend, who had six carries for 33 yards and a TD.</p><p>"I knew these were going to be two tests for us, just being that they were in the [top Red] conference last year," Curie coach Jarve Lewis-Bey said. "But I wasn't expecting this.</p><p>"We knew what they were going to do. They ran the same plays the last three weeks, they ran them this week. We still couldn't stop them."</p>

entries.title: White Sox get needed boost in dramatic game-winning home run from Randal Grichuk
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS – Throughout losing nine of 12 games, matching a season-high four-game skid, and seeing their division lead over the Cleveland Guardians shrink to just half a game, White Sox players and coaches insisted that vibes remained high.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/will-venable-ready-to-adjust-as-needed-as-white-sox-try-to-shake-late-season-funk-colson-montgomery-davis-martin-chase-meidroth-luis-castillo-sean-newcomb" target="_blank" ><u>They professed faith in the brand of baseball</u></a>, the slugging-reliant offense, the piecemeal pitching staff and the loose clubhouse atmosphere that carried them to this point, would pull them out of a mid-September dive before they crashed into the ground. Then 35-year-old Randal Grichuk improbably sprayed a two-out, two-strike, two-run go-ahead opposite-field homer over the right field wall of Busch Stadium, where he began his career 12 years prior.</p><p>After Bryan Hudson pitched a perfect ninth to complete a theft of a 6-5 victory, something akin to all the injuries of a hockey team being revealed after a long postseason run played out in the visitor’s locker room, but in the form of White Sox players admitting how much they needed the moment that Grichuk provided.</p><p>“It was something that we really needed,” said Grichuk. “Hopefully now we can keep playing our game, and be in a lot better place.”</p><p>"I think it can do a lot,” said manager Will Venable of the win.</p><p>It was left unspoken, but it helps that the Guardians lost earlier in the afternoon in Minneapolis, and the White Sox are 1 ½ games up again, and will land in Cleveland on Sunday night still in possession of the American League Central lead.</p><p>“Momentum is a powerful thing,” said Kyle Teel, who came back from an 0-2 count against Cardinals closer Riley O’Brien to walk in front of Grichuk.</p><p>A momentum shift would be good, since the Sox certainly didn’t receive any assurances that all is in working order on Saturday in St. Louis. The 28-man roster is surely not that consumed with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>the club’s amateur scouting director resigning while under internal investigation</u></a>, but the more pressing issue of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/11/white-sox-starter-luis-castillo-feels-hes-very-very-close-to-righting-ship-after-working-on-mechanics-colson-montgomery-strikeout-record-chase-meidroth-joey-bart-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>trade deadline acquisition Luis Castillo’s struggles</u></a> got worse, if anything.</p><p>Pitching behind an opener, Castillo lasted just 2 ⅔ innings and yielded three runs. The damage could have been worse had he not snuck a fastball by Cardinals RBI leader Alec Burleson with the bases loaded to end the fourth; a feat nearly as miraculous as Grichuk’s blast given that Castillo’s velocity had flagged into the low-90s, with no easy answers as to why.</p><p>“I don’t know why because I felt that my mechanics were good, my body feels good,” Castillo said via interpreter.</p><p>It’s a bit late for another skipped start to work further on his delivery.</p><p>“I don't know if we have time to do that again,” said Venable. “The No. 1 thing is to make sure that he's healthy.”</p><p>Venable appeared to shake up his lineup on Saturday, sliding a resurgent Teel near the top of the order, and moving the struggling Colson Montgomery and Braden Montgomery down. But he insisted he was just playing matchups for handedness as always, and not making a reactive late-season switch.</p><p>After second-guessing his own deployment of pinch-hitters in recent days, he was once more back to his aggressive ways, calling Grichuk off the bench to face a lefty in the top of the fourth.</p><p>When it meant that Grichuk wound up in a right-right matchup with O’Brien with two outs in the ninth, another constantly preached element of White Sox baseball emerged: stay on the fastball, even after four-straight sliders put him behind in the count 1-2.</p><p>"He took advantage of a mistake,” Venable said. “We all thought that there was another offspeed coming down below the zone.”</p><p>Sometimes an opponent’s mistake can be the difference, and the Sox were bound–they insisted–to get one eventually.</p><p>“Luckily he left a sinker on over [the plate],” Grichuk said. “Haven’t been able to get that big hit to push us over the top and I know we all feel it. Luckily tonight I was able to come through.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are investigating the death of a woman who was pulled from Lake Michigan on Friday.</p><p>The unidentified woman was pronounced dead after her body was recovered from the water about 8 p.m. near the 300 block of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive, police said.</p><p>Area 3 detectives are conducting an investigation, pending autopsy results, police said. </p><p>No further information was available.</p>

entries.title: Woman, 2 teens wounded in Chicago Lawn shooting
entries.summary: <p>A woman and two teenagers were wounded in a shooting Saturday night in Chicago Lawn, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A 37-year-old woman, a 17-year-old girl, and a 15-year-old boy were standing outside along the 7100 block of South Campbell Avenue at about 6:58 p.m. when two men fired multiple gunshots at them. </p><p>The adult woman suffered gunshot wounds to her head, right hand, and left wrist, police said. </p><p>She was taken to Advocate Christ Medical Center in critical condition, according to police. </p><p>The 15-year-old boy suffered a gunshot wound to his neck and a graze wound to his chest, police said. </p><p>He was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition. </p><p>The 17-year-old girl suffered a gunshot wound to her right knee and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in good condition, according to police.</p><p>The unidentified shooters were last seen in a light-colored sedan, police said.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Police investigate death of 1-year-old girl in West Ridge
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are investigating the death of a 1-year-old girl who was found wounded and unresponsive in West Ridge on Saturday morning, police said.</p><p>The unidentified child was found with visible injuries to her lower body at about 11:40 a.m. along the 2600 block of West Rosemont Avenue, according to police.</p><p>She was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in critical condition, where she died, police said.</p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating the death, police said. An official cause of death has not been determined. <br></p>

entries.title: Bulls Preview: The guard room has talent but will it SLAP when called
entries.summary: <p>They don’t check all the boxes, at least those that new Bulls coach Tiago Splitter and executive vice president Bryson Graham want checked.</p><p>“When you compete on the defense end, your team typically competes harder,” Graham said this offseason.</p><p>Hey, guards, are you listening?</p><p>With Bulls camp a little over two weeks away, the spotlight will be on the backcourt — the starters and the reserves — to see if it can figure out the Splitter way and embrace what he preaches.</p><p>There was progress in that department in the team-only scrimmages in Miami last month, but those scrimmages don’t signify all that much.</p><p>Josh Giddey, Tre Jones, Rob Dillingham and rookie Dailyn Swain need to continue to step up defensively to make sure that Norman Powell, 33, is not left alone on an island.</p><p>That will be the burning question with the guards all fall and into the regular season.</p><p>“I have a vision, I have a way I want to play, but you also have to explore what they do best,” Splitter said recently. “That’s what we’re going to do here.”</p><p>His vision, like Graham’s, focuses on defense and physicality, and on the offensive end, it demands ball movement. Splitter was raised under the Spurs’ umbrella. Ball movement and the extra pass were a way of life.</p><p>That’s where Giddey and Jones can excel.</p><p>Both are pass-first ballhandlers and are from the school of generating the best scoring opportunity.</p><p>The bonus with Giddey is that he also gives Splitter positional size, so he adds rebounding from the backcourt. His 8.3 boards per game last season were a career high.</p><p>Splitter just finished coaching a point forward in Deni Avdija who put up Giddey-like numbers, so there could be some familiarity in several offensive sets.</p><p><b>Backcourt outlook</b></p><p><b>The starters:</b> The Bulls will enter camp with this decision already made. Giddey and Powell will hold down the starting spots in the backcourt. Former coach Billy Donovan liked to give a three-guard look — often because of injuries — but that won’t be the case for the 2026-27 season with the team’s frontcourt bolstered.</p><p><b>Giddey</b> — This is a huge season for him, especially now that he earned the bag in signing a four-year, $100 million deal last offseason. Now it’s about chasing a legacy. This will be the most talent that Giddey has played with since joining the Bulls, and he can be the face of this group reaching expectations.</p><p><b>Powell</b> — If it works with the veteran, great. If it doesn’t, the Bulls have the flexibility to trade Powell to a contender. Powell’s presence has been beyond positive already, and he might be just as important off the court.</p><p><b>The reserves:</b> Jones has shown that he can be a starter by continuing to play winning basketball on a losing team, but after the veteran point guard, there are more questions than answers. That means Dillingham and Swain have some things to prove.</p><p><b>Jones</b> — The consummate pro, Jones is a key reserve for the Bulls and also a key trade piece on the chessboard if the opportunity presents itself.</p><p><b>Swain</b> — It’s hard to erase Summer League from the eyes, but it is reset time for the rookie. Swain could emerge as a defensive presence off the bench and should focus on earning his playing time with that mentality first. That’s how Jimmy Butler got started.</p><p><b>Dillingham</b> — It might be sink-or-swim time for the No. 8 overall pick of the 2024 draft, and Dillingham knows that. He has spent time this offseason working with Powell and is serious about taking the next step.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks coach Jeff Blashill wants to see more puck possession and 'swagger' this season
entries.summary: <p>Jeff Blashill exudes the strongest aura of any <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> coach since Joel Quenneville.</p><p>His personality matches that of a quintessential NHL coach, and he operates with a matching amount of confidence. While Jeremy Colliton was a little too nerdy, Derek King a little too carefree, Luke Richardson a little too nice and Anders Sorensen a little too reserved, Blashill checks boxes with authority.</p><p>The fact he arrived in Chicago with much more previous NHL coaching experience than those four predecessors probably contributes to that. But it's also simply who he is.</p><p>Blashill's actual coaching performance during his first Hawks season was more difficult to assess, though. The team's record (29-39-14) was the second-worst in the league yet their best in five years.</p><p>Entering his second season, the 52-year-old boss he hopes to see his ultra-young roster of players exude an assertive aura of their own.</p><p>"One of the goals that I wanted culturally is to build back our confidence and swagger," Blashill told the Sun-Times this week.</p><p>That influenced the Hawks' big summer splashes. Blashill was involved in both acquiring Bowen Byram and signing Patrick Kane, assisting general manager Kyle Davidson.</p><p>Having previously coached Kane in two world championships, Blashill leaned on that relationship and tried to sell Kane — during his lengthy free agency — on the "talent and character" of the Hawks' young players, many of whom weren't in the league when Kane last played for the Hawks. That evidently worked, and those players now have a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/24/patrick-kane-blackhawks-return-playoffs-connor-bedard-kyle-davidson" target="_blank" >new mentor</a>.</p><p>"[Kane is] going to have a very good impact, and that’s before we start even talking about offensive production," Blashill said. "[That's because of] his impact in the locker room, the example and expectation that he sets, how he approaches every single day in terms of reaching for and demanding excellence."</p><p>The offensive production, of course, should be helpful, too.</p><p>"He feels as good as he has in a long time," Blashill added. "He’s skating well; he’s moving well. Guys that play with their brain first...seem to last a long time in this league, and he certainly has."</p><p>A Byram scouting report, meanwhile, came to Blashill from Sabres assistant coach Seth Appert, a close friend in the industry. That report matched the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/01/blackhawks-bowen-byram-contract-nhl-defensemen-free-agency" target="_blank" >first impression</a> Byram made after the trade: he's a remarkably poised man and defenseman.</p><p>"I think if you get enough guys that are hyper-competitive, have a great inner confidence and swagger and are super detailed about becoming great every day, you’re going to become a way better organization in a hurry," Blashill said.</p><p>Byram's critics argue his risk tolerance is too high, claiming he gives back with defensive unreliability most of what he creates with his dynamic talent. Blashill disagreed.</p><p>"He’s got a skating ability that allows him to attack up the ice, be more active on the rush and in the [offensive] zone, end up around the net we’re attacking and still get back," Blashill said. "That’s a special skill. Not many guys skate like that. Some of the best 'D' in the league are able to do that. A guy like Zach Werenski comes to mind."</p><h3><b>Camp plans</b></h3><p>Blashill is thankful this year isn't his first in charge. It would've been nearly impossible to install entirely new systems in a training camp shortened to less than two weeks.</p><p>Camps around the league start Thursday. The Hawks' preseason opener is Saturday in Minnesota, followed by three more exhibitions next week before the regular-season opener Sept. 29 in Las Vegas.</p><p>With so few practice days between now lacked last season.</p><p>"Whether that’s through winning puck battles, through pressuring to get it back or through support and decision-making with it, that’ll be a really important piece — beyond just getting our systems in place — of what we want to do," Blashill said.</p><p>Blashill discussed the science of gapping (defensemen pressuring opposing puck-carriers in the neutral zone) during exit interviews in April, and he reiterated this week he was "disappointed at the end of the year that we weren’t a better gapping team."</p><p>There were some games last spring in which the Hawks were burned for trying to gap vertically instead of laterally. Blashill believes the team has the potential to improve due to their speed and mobility.</p><p>"[We need to] practice it more," he said. "It’s something we had in our heads last year, but maybe not something we worked on enough."</p><p>Once established inside the offensive zone with possession, Blashill also wants to work on creating scoring chances at a higher rate, since the Hawks were more dangerous off the rush than in the zone last season. He has some tactical changes planned.</p><h3><b>Rookie expectations</b></h3><p>Connor Bedard's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/08/blackhawks-connor-bedard-shoulder-surgery-injury-timeline" target="_blank" >shoulder rehab</a> has progressed to skating on his own, but the Hawks will still have to survive without their superstar for a month or more. They've at least had months to prepare for that situation.</p><p>"A number of our guys are in position to really take steps, and with additions, we’re just a deeper hockey team," Blashill said. "That allows us to be prepared to absorb a significant loss.</p><p>"The power play...might look a little different with and without Bedard. But from a pure playing standpoint, we have a belief in how we want our team to play and how we think we can win long-term with this group, and we’re going to play that way."</p><p>It's unclear if rookie <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/09/blackhawks-anton-frondell-nhl-center-sweden-training-patrick-kane" target="_blank" >Anton Frondell</a> will start as the first-line center in Bedard's spot, but Frondell definitely will start at center, as Davidson foreshadowed back in the spring.</p><p>"[Frondell] played center through most of his life, and then through other people’s decisions, [they] decided to put him on wing," Blashill said. "That’s their prerogative. My decision is, I see him as a guy who has a skill set of a really good winning center. He can play a 200-foot game and still produce offense."</p><p>Fellow rookie <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/29/blackhawks-roman-kantserov-nhl-preparation-english-spencer-knight" target="_blank" >Roman Kantserov</a> will immediately handle a major role, as well. Solely from watching Kantserov's tape from Russia last season, Blashill's expectations have been set high.</p><p>"His ability with the puck [is impressive], both from a passing and shooting aspect," Blashill said. "But he’s also very tenacious, strong on the puck, wins battles, knows how to leverage his body and plays a real complete game. To me, that’s something that allows young players not only to step in and be productive but also to help us win."</p><p>There are two possible news items to monitor this week as camp begins. The first is defenseman Ethan Del Mastro's contract situation, since he remains an unsigned restricted free agent. The second is a captaincy announcement, which — if it happens — will presumably involve Bedard.</p><p>Asked about this season's player leadership structure, Blashill said he has "thought about it," then chuckled as he declined to elaborate further.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: I have big dreams but am struggling to get by
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a person with a million-dollar heart and a 5-cent bank account. I have big dreams that I know could change lives. I want to write a book about my experience with emotional abuse so I can help others heal. I also dream of starting a soda stand to build something tangible with my kids.</p><p>The problem is that my current life is exhausting. I'm raising kids and stepkids, navigating co-parenting drama and working a job I hate just to survive. By the time I finish the daily grind, I'm broke and bone-tired. I know there is more out there for me, but I'm struggling to stay focused when my reality feels like a trap. How can I start these projects when I'm just trying to keep my head above water? I don't want to escape into my dreams; I want to build them. — <i>SODA STAND DREAMER</i></p><p><b>DEAR SODA STAND DREAMER:</b> If you try to write a book and start a business on top of everything else, you may not do any of it well. Choose one dream and put the other on hold for now. If you choose the book, set aside some time each day (or week) and dedicate yourself to writing during that time — no excuses. If you choose the soda stand, get a part-time job at a similar business where you can learn the ropes and earn some startup money. Either dream will require a lot of work and perseverance, but don't give up!</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have a blended family. When he received child support for his daughters, I didn't think it was any of my business what he did with the money. When I received child support for my sons, he thought I should tell him what I spent it on. I don't think it's any of his business. Who's right? Please advise me, as this has been an ongoing argument in our relationship for 20 years. Mind you, our children are grown now with children of their own, and it's time to put this to rest. Who is right? — <i>HAPPILY MARRIED EXCEPT FOR THIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR HAPPILY MARRIED:</b> You are right. You are also entitled to some privacy if it's important to you. In light of the fact that the child support money your husband received was not a subject of discussion, I see no reason why he should feel he has the right to know how you spent yours. What matters in both cases is that the money went toward caring for the children. I truly hope that's what happened.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I was invited to my nephew's wedding in a small town. Without my knowledge, the mother of the groom verbally offered my hotel room to the mother of the bride of a different wedding! (The connection is that they both used the same wedding planner.) When she approached me, I declined to give up my room and move to a different hotel. Subsequently, she unilaterally withdrew my wedding invitation. Am I obligated to send a gift? — <i>TOTALLY STUNNED</i></p><p><b>DEAR STUNNED:</b> What the groom's mother did is appalling, but don't take it out on your nephew unless you have reason to believe he was complicit in these shenanigans.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: What to watch for in Bears-Panthers when each team has the ball
entries.summary: <p><b>WHEN THE </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" ><b>BEARS</b></a><b> HAVE THE BALL</b></p><p>The offseason has been a frenzy of hype about quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, but coach Ben Johnson starts with the rushing attack and the multiplicity of his tight ends. This will be a big game for running back D’Andre Swift and the tight end trio of Colston Loveland, Cole Kmet and Sam Roush.</p><p>Swift could be the Bears’ top weapon. He’s coming off one of his strongest seasons, and he can do more. His head-on running style combined with speed and elusiveness makes him reliable for a few yards at a time and always a threat to take off for an explosive play.</p><p>It’ll be interesting to see how Johnson uses him in the passing game as well. Swift was sixth on the team with 48 targets last season, but when he and Johnson were together with the Lions, Swift got 78 targets in 2021 and 70 the next season.</p><p>Swift is only enhanced by three-tight-end sets, which Johnson will use often because of the confusion they create in defenses. If the Panthers treat those three like wide receivers and try to cover them with defensive backs, the Bears can steamroll a path for Swift out of the backfield.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/04/bears-coach-ben-johnson-now-has-3-premium-talents-at-tight-end-and-his-offense-is-about-to-get-wild" >Johnson was fifth in the NFL in using “13 personnel,”</a> meaning three tight ends, one wide receiver and one running back, and he’s near the forefront of a growing trend. It’s a reasonable estimate that he’ll use it three times as much this season after the Bears invested in Loveland, Kmet and Roush.</p><p><b>WHEN THE PANTHERS HAVE THE BALL</b></p><p>Panthers quarterback Bryce Young is going into his fourth season and has not proved himself. There was improvement last season, but he still finished with the sixth-lowest passer rating (87.8) among players who threw at least 250 passes.</p><p>But here’s what he potentially has going for him against the Bears: Their secondary is patchwork and their defensive line has yet to show it can consistently disrupt quarterbacks.</p><p>Young’s top wide receiver is Tetairoa McMillan, the No. 8 overall pick last season who won offensive rookie of the year with 70 catches for 1,014 yards and seven touchdowns.</p><p>The Bears could simply stick cornerback Jaylon Johnson on him for the day, but at some point the Panthers could get matchups between him and Bears rookie Malik Muhammad. Muhammad, a fourth-round pick, played mostly outside corner in college, but moved to nickel in place of Kyler Gordon.</p><p>The Panthers were 27th in the NFL in total offense (295.6 yards per game) and scoring (18.3 points) last season. They went 0-5 against top-10 defenses and managed an abysmal 11.2 points per game.</p><p>But like most quarterbacks, Young showed he’s capable when he gets time in the pocket. In a win over the Rams, for example, he got pressured just twice on 22 drop-backs and was efficient with 15-for-20 passing, 206 yards, three touchdown passes and a 147.1 passer rating. The Bears were 22nd in pressure percentage and sacks last season.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson will seek another term, says he’s the best progressive choice
entries.summary: <p>After months of deliberation, Mayor Brandon Johnson on Sunday set out on the uphill road to reelection — portraying himself as the only legitimate progressive in the crowded 2027 mayoral race.</p><p>The mayor plans to make the long-awaited announcement Sunday afternoon at the DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center, a nod to his efforts to overturn decades of disinvestment in the Black community, and the need to galvanize support among Black Chicagoans.<b> </b></p><p>Johnson's team is portraying the election as a stark choice for voters: either renew his four-year contract and give him a second chance to tax the rich and deliver for working class residents and African Americans pushing for investment in their long neglected neighborhoods, or return to the days of school closings, shuttered mental health clinics, special interest decision-making, and outsize influence of big business on city government.</p><p>"Chicago voters have an option between the billionaires and the Brandon Johnson coalition, which is a multiracial, intergenerational movement that came together three years ago to elect a working class champion to deliver for working families all across Chicago," said Johnson's political director, Christian Perry. </p><p>Johnson took office boldly proclaiming his intention to become Chicago’s longest-serving mayor. That would have required him to exceed the 22-year reign of Richard M. Daley.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-950000" name="image-950000"></a> <picture </div><p>After a rocky start, Johnson dropped the talk about longevity and began the difficult task of learning on the job. His only prior experience in elected office had been a two-year stint as a Cook County commissioner.</p><p>For months, Johnson fueled speculation that his low poll numbers, his meager campaign fund and his own hesitation to definitively declare for reelection could prompt him to walk away from a second term. On the day before taking his oldest child to college, an emotional Johnson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-second-term-bid-no-decision-yet" >said he wanted to </a>“hold onto this moment” a little longer — both personally and politically.</p><p>By waiting until after Labor Day to announce his decision to run again, Johnson has put himself behind the eight ball. He has less than $650,000 in his campaign fund compared to Giannoulias’ $22 million. Johnson has the power of incumbency and has been making the most of that, but he still needs money to defend his record.</p><p>He doesn’t need to duplicate the $12 million that allowed him to go from single-digit obscurity to the mayor’s office in 2023 in a campaign bankrolled and staffed largely by the Chicago Teachers Union. But he does need enough cash to run costly television ads.</p><p>“We're still living in a time where broadcast TV ads are important. They haven't become irrelevant,” said longtime Democratic strategist Joanna Klonsky, a close advisor to then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot. </p><p>“Brandon Johnson's core strength in 2023 was that he had a ground army of volunteers who were willing to get out there and knock doors for him. But he still will have to do paid media advertising if he's going to win the election… That is going to take a heck of a lot more money than he has on hand right now.”</p><h3>The SEIU factor in the campaign</h3><p>Four years ago, Johnson had a powerful coalition of progressive labor unions that included the CTU, where he started as a community organizer and the Service Employees International Union Locals 1, 73 and Healthcare.</p><p>But the CTU’s failed attempt to take over SEIU non-teaching jobs at the Chicago Board of Education broke apart that powerful coalition. SEIU, which contributed $4.5 million to Johnson’s first mayoral campaign, is now expected to pull its support of Johnson. That could cost the mayor millions and shrink his army of political foot soldiers who knock on doors, distribute campaign literature and work the phones.</p><p>All of that leaves Johnson in a hole from which he needs to climb out.</p><p>CTU President Stacy Davis Gates failed to get her members to raise their dues at a time when winning a majority on the newly elected school board and electing a board president is an equally important priority. But because she also serves as president of the Illinois Federation of Teachers, she can draw from those funds as well. And, she said, “my union always does the impossible.”</p><p>“The question of money is always one where we're going to lose the arms race,” Davis Gates said. “But we have a membership that is over 80% women, where we pool our resources together, and we do the best that we can through phone banking. We do the best that we can through canvassing. We do the best that we can through influencing our friends and our family to understand these issues and dimension.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Four years ago, Johnson carried a second-place finish into the runoff and managed to defeat Paul Vallas by highlighting his conservative views in a heavily Democratic city that leans progressive. Vallas had run for governor once as a Democrat, but his own conservative viewpoints on social media were his undoing.</p><p>The incumbent mayor is expected to try to do the same to Giannoulias. On the day after Giannoulias entered the race,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandon-johnson/2026/08/03/johnson-blasts-mayoral-rival-giannoulias-without-naming-him" > Johnson said the same billionaire business interests</a> that closed schools and mental health clinics under former Mayor Rahm Emanuel are trying to “take us back to a time of trauma and torment,” and declared that Chicago is “not going back.”</p><p>Former Ald. Pat O’Connor (40th), who served as unofficial floor leader under Daley and Emanuel, said Johnson’s attempts to portray Giannoulias as the reincarnation of Emanuel will not work.</p><p>“If he comes out to dirty up Giannoulias, or he tries to dirty up [mayoral candidate and U.S. Rep. Mike] Quigley, they don’t lean left, but they are clearly not conservative and they are not going to be people you can put basically into a corner like Vallas — who is on record saying ‘I am truly a Republican.’ His own words were enough to put him in that spot. You won’t find that with Giannoulias. You’re not going to find that with Quigley,” O’Connor said.</p><p>Eric Adelstein, a media strategist for Giannoulias, said he’s bracing for Johnson to “run as far to the left as he can” and portray himself as “a mayor who’s for the little guy against the big guy.”</p><p>“The problem is people believe that’s where his heart is, but they don’t believe he’s been very successful at it and they’re just hungry for leadership,” Adelstein said.</p><p>Adelstein expects Johnson to attempt to portray Giannoulias as “some out of touch caricature,” but says that will fall flat because his client is “building a coalition that includes business and labor and electeds and community folks.”</p><h3>Johnson’s advantage — the affordability card</h3><p>Johnson’s advantage is that he has the progressive lane to himself at a time when affordability is everything. As he embarks on his final budget, he’ll likely renew his failed efforts to tax the rich and dare the City Council to shoot his proposal down again.</p><p>On the campaign trail, he is certain to tout his biggest accomplishment on his progressive revenue to-do list: a tax on social media companies that is expected to generate a windfall of $49.2 million this year, nearly 60% above the city’s original estimate.</p><p>Most of Johnson’s progressive legislative accomplishments came in his first year in office when he pushed through the most generous paid leave policy in the country, reinstated the city’s Department of Environment, and laid the groundwork to reopen shuttered mental health clinics.</p><p>More recently, he has offered renter protections and is pushing for a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" > moratorium on the construction of new data centers</a> to attract progressive voters, many of whom live on the North Side and along the lakefront.</p><p>Johnson will also benefit from the fact that crime is down in Chicago. The city saw 122 murders in June, July and August, the lowest summer total since 1965, according to city and police data. Johnson will tout investments he has made in youth jobs and in violence prevention workers who work to<b> </b><b> </b>de-escalate gun violence.</p><p>In 2023, Johnson finished second on the strength of his performance with young progressives along the north lakefront, the hipster Milwaukee Avenue corridor and left-leaning hubs on the Northwest Side. He didn’t win a single majority-Black ward in the first round, before winning every majority-Black ward in the runoff against Vallas.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/5/23671882/brandon-johnson-analysis-mayor-victory-democratic-playbook-chicago-vallas" >How Johnson did it: Flawless execution of ‘smart typical playbook in Chicago politics’ won mayoral race</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>This time, Johnson has to consolidate the Black vote immediately to stand a chance at making the runoff. That’s in part because at least some north lakefront voters appear to be disappointed with Johnson.</p><p>“It's a fickle voting bloc,” Klonsky said. “They have turned on people that they've voted for on a number of occasions in recent years... Those early stages of the Johnson administration, where things were really chaotic and difficult… that's when he lost some of those voters, and it's been hard to get them back. It's not a foregone conclusion that he can't get them back, but time is running out.”</p><p>It hasn’t been all rosy with African American voters either. Johnson himself acknowledged recently that he paid the price for the difficult choices he was forced to make during the migrant crisis that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/22/migrant-crisis-chicago-cost-inspector-general-david-glockner-report" >cost the city $639.6 million.</a> It reignited an us-versus-them conflict between Black and Latino Chicagoans.</p><p>“I understand the frustration that Black people felt during that mission." I do. I do,” Johnson said in July. “Here’s what I understand: We don’t ask for much. We don’t. We just don’t want our schools to close. We want opportunities for paid jobs... For Black Chicago in particular, it kind of felt [like] government was able to turn on resources in a moment’s notice — and our communities have been starved for decades.”</p><p>Cook County Commissioner Tara Stamps, a former Johnson campaign chairman and close ally, said Black Chicagoans may have lingering resentments about the migrant crisis, but the damage done “calls for repair, not abandonment.”</p><p>“I'm not going to leave my husband because he pissed me off. I'm not going to divorce myself from my children because they disappointed me,” said Stamps, who served as Johnson’s mentor teacher at Jenner Elementary School. In June 2023, she took his seat on the county board.</p><p>“If it's anything that I can say to Black people in this moment, if you think it's anybody else other than Brandon Johnson that has the Black community at heart, you are not paying attention, and it will be a mistake to put your vote and your confidence in anybody other than Brandon Johnson if you are trying to preserve and maintain anything, any kind of Black identity in this city.”</p><h3>How is Johnson polling?</h3><p>Sources said Johnson’s own polling shows his public approval rating among Black voters plunged to 28% in early 2024. More recently it stood somewhere between 48% and 52% in those same polls.</p><p>If the migrant crisis was a low point for Johnson politically, Operation Midway Blitz was a high-water mark. It showcased Johnson as a champion for Chicagoans and their first line of defense against the Trump administration.</p><p>When Chicagoans were being swept off streets and entire neighborhoods raided by ICE agents, Johnson signed a series of executive orders aimed at thwarting their efforts and holding them accountable. In the year leading up to the deportation campaign, Johnson flew to Washington D.C. to defend Chicago at a U.S. House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing in March 2025, and he has gone toe-to-toe with President Donald Trump on multiple occasions.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" name="image-030000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54003bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+630/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fe1%2F4552484a4b3bbe887c1fc60dad2d%2Faptopix-immigration-chicago.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c0f66de/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+630/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fe1%2F4552484a4b3bbe887c1fc60dad2d%2Faptopix-immigration-chicago.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8eea794/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5998x3366+0+630/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3a%2Fe1%2F4552484a4b3bbe887c1fc60dad2d%2Faptopix-immigration-chicago.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="ICE agents detain a protester as other protesters try to stop them in East Side, Chicago, Tuesday, Oct. 14, 2025. Mike Rodriguez (22nd), who represents the Little Village neighborhood that was targeted repeatedly by federal authorities, said Johnson has a compelling story to tell Latino voters.</p><p>“While our voting numbers have lagged behind other communities, we are a sleeping giant, and our community has been waking up and will continue to be waking up and be more of an electoral force,” said Rodriguez,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/09/09/ald-mike-rodriguez-22nd-ward-not-seeking-re-election-brandon-johnson-city-council-ally" > who recently announced </a>he will not seek re-election.</p><p>Turnout will be a major factor, as it was four years ago, when Johnson made the runoff by capturing just 21.6% of the 35.8% of registered voters who showed up at the polls.</p><p>"A lot of people have gotten to the point where, if they don’t care about either candidate, they stay home,” said O’Connor. “That’s how you get people who are truly unqualified and should be very unpopular, but their unpopularity at that point is a benefit to them because people stay away.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/07/08/one-of-mayor-brandon-johnson-most-ardent-city-council-adversaries-wont-seek-reelection-in-2027" >Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn</a> (13th) learned the political game from his mentor, now-convicted former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan. He predicts that Johnson will make the runoff and lose to whomever his opponent turns out to be.</p><p>Quinn says that most voters he talks to consider Johnson a “nice guy that isn’t up to running the city.”</p><p>But it would be a mistake to write him off.</p><p>“His path to victory is that he needs a robust turnout in [Democratic Socialist] wards," Quinn said. "He needs to rely heavily on the teachers union and lean on older African Americans, and he needs to present a clean, crisp reason for why Chicagoans should give him another four years.”</p>

entries.title: Review: Swedish pop icon Robyn is a dancing queen as she brings her Sexistential tour to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Robyn is still dancing on her own. At least, she did so for nearly two hours Saturday night at the United Center. With a backing band of synth-pop wizards perched on a platform behind her, the Swedish pop star was out in the open on a center thrust stage, doing her trademark shimmy and singing to the rafters on numbers like her 2010 megahit.</p><p>All these years later, the song still remains the collective breakup song of millennials. In Chicago, they even earned Robyn’s personal round of applause and the “loudest so far of the tour” honor for singing the chorus with gusto during an a capella break at the top of the track.</p><p>But something feels different about how Robyn moves to it now. Sixteen years and some substantial life changes later, “dancing on my own” feels like an act of defiance. Like she purposefully chooses it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6d0000" name="image-6d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9f76b9b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8033x4508+0+425/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2Fe5%2F5eda349c4d62821e62ace2c18af2%2Frobyn-260914-30.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/310635d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8033x4508+0+425/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2Fe5%2F5eda349c4d62821e62ace2c18af2%2Frobyn-260914-30.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9e7955c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8033x4508+0+425/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff5%2Fe5%2F5eda349c4d62821e62ace2c18af2%2Frobyn-260914-30.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Robyn hits the stage on The Sexistential Tour stop in Chicago at the United Center, Saturday, September 12, 2026. Get a life. Grow up. … Because life is really, really embarrassing. It never turns out the way you thought it would. And then you die,” she abruptly added, voicing her internal concerns about how she had come to a crossroads in her career and personal life upon that album's release and subsequently took nearly a decade away to figure out her next steps. But there was a silver lining, Robyn said, sharing her journey to becoming a single mother after having her son Tyko via IVF in 2023. “But then I had a baby. I had a child. And I leaned into it, as they say. I don’t know if it makes sense. But what I’m really trying to say is thank you all for listening throughout all these years.”</p><p>Naturally, the speech was met with a huge swell of applause from the sold-out crowd, many of whom have been by Robyn’s side for 30 years and all her eras. From her tender “Show Me Love” R&B breakout in 1997 to the bold alt-pop career resurgence of “Dancing On My Own”to now finding Robyn in her “Sexistential” phase of reclaiming life on her terms, the pop queen has always met her audience where they’re at. And she’s also stayed relevant by gathering new followers along the way who are hungry for a voice that soothes their ennui.</p><p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2025/08/01/gracie-abrams-lollapalooza-performance-review" target="_blank" ><u>Gracie Abrams brought out Robyn</u></a> as the guest star of her Lollapalooza set in 2025, the massive response was a cross-generational awakening. It spilled over recently when fellow Swede Zara Larsson cross-collaborated with Robyn on remixes of each other’s songs, “Puss Puss” and “Talk to Me.” Because, as even Larsson knows, across the Swedish biggest stages of her career and teaming up with a hand-picked opener in each city. Chicago was lucky enough to get feminist icon Peaches, who set a tone of bravado for the rest of the night. Putting the “sex” in “Sexistential,” the always-outrageous performer staged a show that rivaled GWAR’s penchant for fake appendages and varying levels of nudity, all astutely camouflaged with some very strategic placement of tape and strobe light effects. Over 30 short minutes, Peaches dove into her electro-rap classics like “F--- Your Face” (“with consent,” she clarified), the anti-establishment protest song “Flip This” and the queer anthem “Boys Wanna Be Her,” with all of the numbers espousing the liberation that Robyn preaches on her new album. </p><p>“Sexistential” is rampant with messages about desire and sensuality, womanhood and single motherhood and ultimately finding yourself again through the things that you love about life. Robyn performed most of the songs from the album, earning high points for the pop thunder of “Really Real” and the more downtempo “Dopamine,” which she performed lying down on a rotating part of the stage that twirled her like a carousel to match the dizzying thoughts of her own emotions.</p><p>The stage set, too, was meant to evoke the album’s confessional nature. There were no distracting videos or props to take away focus and no compartmentalized acts to take away the flow. The only add-on was a large pair of flowing white curtains that moved when a breeze hit, giving the feeling of looking through an open window and seeing Robyn in her bedroom as she processed her innermost thoughts. She often changed stage outfits in this open environment too, another gateway to finding the singer at her most vulnerable.</p><p>All of it was setting up for the final moments of the show where Robyn wrapped with “Dancing on My Own” and a shower of glitter rained down on her. It was the final act of redemption and of finding her sparkle again.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-390000" name="image-390000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d44dc5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fec%2F0d5fb186434a9d77367a0d7193b4%2Frobyn-260914-19.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2e408d7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fec%2F0d5fb186434a9d77367a0d7193b4%2Frobyn-260914-19.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f9b38d7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ffa%2Fec%2F0d5fb186434a9d77367a0d7193b4%2Frobyn-260914-19.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Robyn hits the stage on The Sexistential Tour stop in Chicago at the United Center, Saturday, September 12, 2026. entries.title: Bears move past nightmarish start to season to lead Panthers 14-7 at end of first quarter
entries.summary: <p>CHARLOTTE, N.C. — It's been a chaotic and mistake-filled first quarter for the Bears, but they're up 14-7 on the Panthers thanks to running back D'Andre Swift and quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>.</p><p>The Bears committed three penalties, lost a fumble, had two glaring lapses in pass coverage and got flagged for a short kickoff, but Swift has been unstoppable in his first game since signing a three-year, $33.8 million contract extension and Williams connected with Rome Odunze for a spectacular pass.</p><p>Swift has eight carries for 65 yards and a touchdown, which he scored with 1:59 left in the quarter to put the Bears ahead. Williams, meanwhile, is 5-of-6 passing for 88 yards and has a nine-yard touchdown scramble.</p><p>Before the game, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> made backup quarterback Tyson Bagent inactive because of a back injury, though he's available as the emergency third quarterback if Williams and Case Keenum get hurt.</p><p>Safety Xavier Woods is out with a groin injury he suffered in practice last week. That puts the Bears in a tough spot as top safety Coby Bryant is out for most or all of the season and the other starter is rookie Dillon Thieneman making his NFL debut. The Bears likely will start Cam Lewis for Woods.</p><p>Here are the Bears' inactives:</p><p>QB Tyson Bagent (back)<br>QB Miller Moss<br>LT Ozzy Trapilo (knee)<br>OL Jordan McFadden</p><p>DL Jayden Loving<br>DL Jamree Kromah<br>S Xavier Woods (groin)</p>

entries.title: Postal service truck stolen in the Loop
entries.summary: <p>A man stole a United States Postal Service truck Saturday evening in the Loop. Chicago police said. </p><p>A USPS worker exited the mail truck to make a delivery around 7:50 p.m. in the 1100 block of South State Street when the man got in the truck and drove away. The worker called police, and officers spotted the truck and tried to pull it over. But the truck didn't stop and sideswiped a car trying to flee, according to police.</p><p>Officers later spotted the truck again in traffic and stopped it. The man got out and was arrested. Police said no one was injured.<br></p>

entries.title: Is truth whatever you want it to be?
entries.summary: <p>If you look down enough alleys in Chicago, you will eventually see a cellist in a bowler hat. I know this is true, based on personal experience. In 2015, I was at the Glenwood Avenue Arts Festival in Rogers Park, heard the distinctive low rosined rumbling of a cello, turned my head and saw this fellow and his instrument.</p><p>I later wrote something. At the time, I thought it was a story about ignorance, which has its own attractions, and knowledge, which bears its own disappointments.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>This is how I explained it:</p><p>"When you are confronted with something enigmatic, you can do one of two things. You can either keep going about your business, accepting the gift of its mystery. Or you can investigate, plunge into the thicket, push aside the leaves of the puzzle and try to find the truth within. The former is probably the better path for a life imbued with tantalizing possibility and, even, magic. Had I kept walking, i would forever wonder."</p><p>I didn't keep walking; I found out and wrote <a class="Link" href="https://www.everygoddamnday.com/2015/08/enigma-spotted-in-alley.html" target="_blank" >a blog post</a>. When I stumbled upon it after more than a decade, something struck me, something more important that I missed at the time.</p><p>The opening sentence is a lie.</p><p>Most people, no matter how many alleys they gaze down, will <i>never</i> see a cellist in a bowler hat.</p><p>What made me think otherwise? Made me believe a clear falsehood is actually a general truism? Easy. Because it happened to me. The fog of personal experience blinds us. Push someone with a strong opinion —immigrants out! —as to why they feel that way, and you inevitably find some minor incident. They were disturbed by music being blasted late a night, magnified into unshakable conviction because it happened to them.</p><p>I crafted the opening sentence in 2015, affected by what had just happened. To me. But you weren't there; so why did you accept it? And I bet you did. You didn't stop, pound your fist and say, "No! I'm never going to see that."</p><p>Why? Well, you read it in a newspaper. A trusted source. There is a photograph, right there, of a cellist in a bowler hat, in an alley. For all the AI hubbub, you don't distrust your eyes. Perhaps most importantly: the lie conjures up the romantic image of a city of unlimited possibility we want to embrace. Leading to an important truth: we believe what we want to believe.</p><p>That's why Donald Trump lying is no big deal — not to me, or to anyone else. Did he just offer every American $5,000 if the Republicans win the midterms? And immediately killjoy journalists began toting up all the unfulfilled Trump bribe promises — the DOGE refund, the tariff compensation and so on.</p><p>Completely missing the point: The purpose of this continual lying isn't to make us believe any one given untruth. It's to undermine the value of truth and falsehood. I believe Trump could promise to burn every church in America to the ground if the midterms go his way, and he wouldn't lose a Republican vote. Because they're not processing anything he says anymore. Or as I've written before: Once you get in the habit of ignoring reality, the exact nature of the reality being ignored hardly matters.</p><p>Short term. But long term, truth has consequences.</p><p>Our summer was scoured by storms and fires that are going to get worse and worse because what Al Gore called "An Inconvenient Truth," at least too inconvenient for people who sell coal and gasoline. </p><p>Vaccines are essential and lifesaving. Having a president and secretary of health who think otherwise lights the fuse on a time bomb. In six months or a year, when diseases that we contained decades ago are scything through elementary schools across the country, parents will look up, aghast, and wonder, "How could we have believed them?" Because they wanted to, a lesson learned too late to bring their children back.</p><p>Yes, certain lies are stylistic — an excuse I'll use to forgive myself the cellist fib. Untruth can be a story, harmless entertainment, like going to the opera and enjoying ourselves, even though there was no Carmen, no cigarette factory, no bullfight.</p><p>What's wrong with believing anything can happen? That if you wait on a Chicago street corner long enough, an elephant will walk by. It did happen, once — July 2, 1943, Judy the Elephant refused to get into a truck at the Brookfield Zoo, so the 7,200 pound pachyderm was walked the 18 miles up First Avenue, along Washington Boulevard, all the way to the Lincoln Park Zoo.</p><p>Well, for starters, if you plan on camping out now, waiting for the next one, it'll be a long wait.</p>

entries.title: 22-year-old man fatally shot in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>A 22-year-old man was fatally shot early Sunday in the Fuller Park neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man was inside a car at around 4 a.m. in the 4200 block of South Wentworth Avenue when two cars pulled up alongside and several people in both vehicles fired shots at the man, according to police.. The man, shot in his chest and shoulder, was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p>
